justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across horizons, anchored near the 48–49 range at the one-day mark and gradually rising toward 48.6 at one month. At the one-day horizon, the estimate is tightly grounded in recent price momentum, mean-reversion tendencies, and the assumption that no major macro catalyst will materialize overnight. The slight upward tilt at one week and one month reflects a mild bullish bias built from trend continuation signals — perhaps modest positive carry, slowly improving sentiment, or a gradual fundamental tailwind — while acknowledging that markets rarely move in straight lines. In the absence of a strong directional signal, the estimates stay close to the prevailing level with only small incremental adjustments.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a standard consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, intraday volatility is relatively predictable and bounded by recent realized volatility, so the 90% interval spans roughly two percentage points. By one week, event risk accumulates — scheduled data releases, central bank communications, or geopolitical developments can shift the distribution meaningfully — widening the interval to about 3.6 points. At one month, the range opens further to 7.2 points, reflecting the full spectrum of macro scenarios that could plausibly unfold, including shifts in growth expectations, inflation surprises, or credit market stress.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an abrupt risk-off episode — triggered by a financial stability event, an unexpected hawkish policy shift, or a geopolitical shock — could push prices through the lower bound of even the one-month interval. Liquidity gaps or forced deleveraging could amplify such moves in a nonlinear way that historical volatility estimates would understate. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected policy pivot, a blowout earnings or economic data surprise, or a short-squeeze dynamic could propel prices beyond the 52 level, especially over the monthly horizon.

It is also worth acknowledging model risk itself as a source of tail exposure. The estimates assume a relatively stable volatility regime and rely implicitly on recent historical patterns remaining informative. Structural breaks — changes in correlation regimes, sudden liquidity withdrawal, or macro regime shifts — are by definition underrepresented in backward-looking inputs. These tail scenarios are not fully captured in the stated intervals, meaning the true distribution has somewhat fatter tails than the confidence bounds suggest.
